resources.string: How ventricular cilia move nearby fluid
A schematic of the normal ventricular lining and nearby cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Mouse studies inform the local flow example. Size and motion are not to scale.
Ependymal cells lie side by side along the walls of the brain ventricles. Their apical surfaces face the fluid-filled space; brain tissue lies beneath the cells.
Many motile cilia project from each cell into the ventricle. Each beats from a fixed base, sweeping one way and bending as it returns.
The beats form a traveling wave
Neighbors beat with a slight timing offset. This makes a metachronal wave: the pattern moves along the lining, but the cilia stay anchored to their own cells.
Together, the beating cilia can move a nearby layer of CSF along the lining. The dots trace that local motion; they do not show flow throughout the ventricle.

Studies of the mouse third ventricle found that patches of cilia can guide fluid in different directions. The choroid plexus makes most CSF, and other forces such as pulsations also move it on a larger scale.
Ciliated cross-section of the ventricular lining
This space contains cerebrospinal fluid. Only a small region of one ventricular wall is shown.
Tufts project into the fluid, where their coordinated beats influence flow close to the wall.
Each cilium is rooted at the apical surface, the side of the cell facing the ventricle.
Neighboring cells meet side by side to form a lining one cell thick in this section.
The lining sits directly against neural tissue on the side away from the ventricular cavity.
